title: Why a startup always needs more money than planned, even if you plan for it
summary: Jason Cohen argues that investors are right to say "raise more than you think you need." Any deviation from plan, whether revenue grows slower or faster, requires more cash than the base plan. Since you can't predict finances 18 months out, raising only the planned amount creates a cash crunch 9-12 months in.

principles.text: You only need the planned amount of money if everything goes exactly to plan; any deviation, up or down, costs more.
principles.quote: The only way you need the actual amount of money you thought you needed, is if everything in the next 18 months goes exactly according to plan--a deviation *in either direction* means you need more money.

principles.text: If growth lags plan, you've already committed to costs and should keep going, which burns more cash than planned.
principles.quote: You're burning more money than you expected, but the correct course of action is to forge ahead and let revenue catch up, not fire half your team and retreat.

principles.text: Faster-than-planned growth also drains cash, because new customers cost more upfront than their early revenue and you must hire ahead.
principles.quote: You incur customer on-boarding costs faster than planned, so although in the long-run your revenue will more than make up for it, right now these unexpected new customers cost much more than their revenue contributions, and cash reserves plummet.

principles.text: Customer acquisition costs rise faster than revenue, so growth itself needs a cash investment.
principles.quote: It costs money to acquire a customer, but takes time for the monthly revenue to cover those costs, therefore costs rise faster than revenue, so you need a cash investment to fund that growth.

principles.text: Precisely predicting startup finances 18 months out is delusional; raising only the planned amount denies that and creates a cash crunch.
principles.quote: You're delusional if you think you can predict your startup's finances 18 months out with precision!

principles.text: Treat money needs like Hofstadter's Law: a business takes more money than expected even after accounting for that.
principles.quote: A business always takes more money than you expect, even when you take this fact into account.
